text: Edelheit says historians have not stressed enough the differences between Ficino and Pico, whom they sometimes treat as two equal and similar representatives of Florentine humanism or philosophy.

quotes.text: Historians of the intellectual life of the period have not always emphasized enough the differences between Ficino and Pico, who were regarded sometimes as two equal, and similar, representatives of humanism and/or philosophy in Florence in our period.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 41' at l. 2217 opens this page

bears_on.note: Edelheit's framing: the two thinkers should be distinguished, not paired

judged.justification: Refines the paired 'Florentine Platonists' picture by insisting on divergence.

text: Edelheit contrasts the two: Ficino, in On the Christian Religion, offers a historical picture of religion and of Christianity's place in it built on newly arrived Neoplatonic texts and ignores the doctrines of the Doctors, whereas Pico's Apology is concerned with purifying religious opinions and beliefs.

quotes.text: Ficino, in his On the Christian Religion, offers a new historical picture of religion, and of the unique place of Christianity in it, based on newly arrived Neoplatonic texts, both pagan and Christian. He does not examine in detail any of the views and dogmas of the Doctors of the Church, but simply ignores them in most of his work
quotes.page_basis: running head '42 introduction' at l. 2265 opens this page

quotes.text: Pico, on the other hand, is not concerned in his Apology with Church organization and other social phenomena, but mainly with the purification of religious opinions and beliefs.
quotes.page_basis: running head '42 introduction' at l. 2265 opens this page

bears_on.note: Edelheit contrasts Ficino's Neoplatonic history of religion with Pico's critical purification of opinion

judged.justification: Sets the two theologies side by side on aim and method.

text: Edelheit says Pico's mastery of scholastic philosophy, in which he was far more expert than Ficino, allowed him to show theologians in their own terms how fragile some scholastic dogmas were, and that he appealed not to a dogmatic philosophy such as Platonism but to the doubting method of the skeptical Academy.

quotes.text: His mastery of scholastic philosophy—in which he was far more an expert than Ficino—enables him to show the theologians, in their own terms and modes of thought, how fragile and contradictory some of the scholastic dogmas and sententiae, even those of the most respected saints and Doctors, can be.
quotes.page_basis: running head '42 introduction' at l. 2265 opens this page

quotes.text: he appeals, not to an ancient dogmatic philosophy such as Platonism (not to mention the Aristotelianism of the scholastics), but to the doubting and searching method of the skeptical Academy.
quotes.page_basis: running head '42 introduction' at l. 2265 opens this page

bears_on.note: Pico the greater scholastic, and not a Platonist by method, on Edelheit's reading

judged.justification: Puts Pico's difference from Ficino in his scholastic training and Academic method.

text: Edelheit argues that treating Ficino and Pico alike as continuers of scholasticism, because both use scholastic terms and procedures, disregards the difference in their scholastic education and their aim in using such terms.

quotes.text: The attempt to present both Pico and Ficino as practitioners of the scholasitc tradition—because both of them employ some scholastic terms and procedures—amounts to disregarding both the differences in their scholastic education and their aim in using such scholastic terms.
quotes.page_basis: running head '42 introduction' at l. 2265 opens this page

bears_on.note: Against reading the two as one scholastic tradition

text: Edelheit argues that Pico uses scholastic literature and argument in the Apology only in answering the papal commission, to show his technical competence, while his own account of theology and religion uses a different Latin style and arguments linking the ancient Academy's skepticism with faith.

quotes.text: he does use scholastic literature and forms of argumentation, but only in his critical responses to the accusations of the theologians who were members of the papal commission, in order to demonstrate to them his competence in technical theological discussions and to refute their arguments on their own ground.
quotes.page_basis: running head '20 introduction' at l. 1203 opens this page

quotes.text: But when he presents his own attitude to theology and religion, Pico uses a very different Latin style, and he also uses philosophical arguments which connect the skepticism of the ancient Academy, on the philosophical level, with faith and opinions which appear only in Scripture and in the primitive Church.
quotes.page_basis: running head '20 introduction' at l. 1203 opens this page

bears_on.note: The commission's accusers are the audience for Pico's scholastic idiom

judged.justification: Reads Pico's scholasticism as tactical, addressed to his accusers, rather than as his own philosophical position.

text: Edelheit says Pico, when he wrote his Apology, put Scripture and revelation as the true foundation of Christianity, and did so more explicitly than Ficino.

quotes.text: Pico, at the time he wrote his Apology, emphasized (and in an even more explicit way than Ficino) Scripture and revelation as the true foundation of Christianity.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 21' at l. 1248 opens this page

bears_on.note: Edelheit's comparison of Ficino and Pico on the foundation of Christianity

text: Edelheit says Ficino and Pico, Ficino in practice and Pico more explicitly and methodically, tried to redraw the line between dogmas with divine sanction and later disputable opinions, and relied on the earliest Fathers such as Augustine and Origen in doing so.

quotes.text: Humanists like Ficino and Pico—the first in his practice, the second more explicitly and methodically—attempted to redraw the line between dogmas which had full divine sanction and later opinions, which were disputable and subject to criticism and rejection.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 35' at l. 1930 opens this page

quotes.text: Ficino and Pico often rely on some of the earliest Fathers, such as Augustine and Origen, who were closer to early Christianity than the Doctors and later saints.
quotes.page_basis: running head '36 introduction' at l. 1977 opens this page

bears_on.note: Shared method of separating dogma from opinion, differing in explicitness

text: Edelheit connects Pico, Ficino and Savonarola through the subordination of church rulings to revelation: Pico, in the Origen discussion, makes the decrees of councils subordinate to revelation, Ficino builds his theology on revelation such as prophecies and miracles, and Savonarola claimed direct divine inspiration and that even the pope could err.

quotes.text: It is quite clear from Pico’s discussion of the salvation of Origen—where he maintains that a special revelation is the sole criterion for determining whether or not Origen was saved—that for him the decrees of binding Church councils were subordinated to revelation. This is what connects him, on the one hand, to Ficino, who bases his own humanist theology on moments of revelation such as prophecies and miracles, and, on the other, to the preacher and prophet Savonarola, who claimed to be subject to direct inspiration from God and who maintained that even the pope could err.

bears_on.note: Common ground on revelation as criterion
Common ground on revelation over conciliar and papal authority

judged.justification: Sets Pico between Ficino and Savonarola on the authority of revelation.

text: Edelheit says Pico, who wrote the famous speech later titled De hominis dignitate, was regarded by Poliziano and Barbaro as a member of their intellectual milieu, so that on Kristeller's approach he would be excluded from humanism for being too involved in philosophy and scholasticism.

quotes.text: Pico, who wrote one of the most representative documents of the new humanist culture, the famous speech which was later entitled De hominis dignitate, and who was regarded by contemporary humanists such as Poliziano and Barbaro as a member of their “intellectual milieu”, should—if we adopt this approach of Kristeller’s—be excluded from the humanist movement since he was too involved in philosophy and in contemporary scholasticism
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 11' at l. 751 opens this page

bears_on.note: Poliziano counted Pico among his intellectual milieu, per Edelheit

text: Edelheit reports Schmitt's view that Pico, by proposing the harmony of Plato and Aristotle among other theses, went beyond Ficino's notion of two unbroken traditions of truth, so that truth for Pico resides in many traditions.

quotes.text: Pico proposed other theses to defend, including the harmony between Plato and Aristotle. It is precisely here that he went beyond Ficino’s notion of twin unbroken traditions of philosophical and theological truth. Truth, instead of residing in two traditions only, resides in many.
quotes.page_basis: running head '8 introduction' at l. 606 opens this page

bears_on.note: Schmitt's contrast between Ficino's two traditions and Pico's many, reported by Edelheit

text: Edelheit reports Trexler's model that both Lorenzo de' Medici, as patron of culture and humanism, and Savonarola tried to reform the nature of public rituals, and offers it as an example of connecting culture to religion, though he prefers to focus on the theology of Ficino and Pico.

quotes.text: Trexler believes that this model can explain the relation between Lorenzo de’ Medici, the patron of culture and humanism, and the Dominican Savonarola. Both of them, each one in his own way, attempted to reform the very nature of rituals in public life.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 39' at l. 2125 opens this page

bears_on.note: Lorenzo and Savonarola compared by Trexler
Savonarola and Lorenzo compared by Trexler

text: Edelheit holds that Ficino and Pico share a sense of crisis, reject scholastic approaches to religion, and draw on newly discovered pagan philosophies, but that their attempts at a new theology part ways and give very different results.

quotes.text: They both share a sense of crisis, and both feel that there ... is a need for a new, and purer, kind of Christianity. They both reject the scholastic approaches to the nature of religion. They are both influenced by newly discovered philosophies originating in pagan antiquity, and make use of them in attempting to constitute a purer theology.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 41' at l. 2217 opens this page

quotes.text: But here the ways part.
quotes.page_basis: running head '42 introduction' at l. 2265 opens this page

bears_on.note: Shared aims, divergent methods, in Edelheit's account

judged.justification: Frames the relation as shared aims with divergent methods.

text: Edelheit says Ficino's Platonic Theology contains hidden echoes of Aquinas's Summa contra Gentiles, the only scholastic text that contemporary sources expressly say Ficino studied, and takes the lack of express references as evidence of Ficino's attitude.

quotes.text: Some ... hidden references to Thomas Aquinas’ Summa contra Gentiles (the only scholastic text which we are expressly told in contemporary sources was studied by Ficino) in the Platonic Theology is, if anything, evidence of this position. Otherwise, why have these echoes without express references?
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 43' at l. 2312 opens this page

warrants.text: Argues from the absence of express references to the presence of echoes

bears_on.note: Ficino's limited and silent scholastic reading, against Pico's

text: Edelheit reports Allen's description of Ficino's On the Christian Religion as an explicitly apologetic work written after Ficino's admission to the priesthood that avoids many of his characteristically Platonic ideas, and says he will give a different interpretation.

quotes.text: According to Allen this work is “… an explicitly apologetic work written after Ficino’s admission to the priesthood and studiously avoids many of his characteristically Platonic ideas”.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 13' at l. 847 opens this page

quotes.text: I shall ... present a different interpretation of this work and its importance in chapter three of this book.
quotes.page_basis: running head '14 introduction' at l. 901 opens this page

bears_on.note: Debate over how Platonic Ficino's theology of religion is

text: Edelheit says Ficino was, at the start of Savonarola's reforms, one of Savonarola's supporters, and traces a sense of crisis developing from Caroli through Ficino's early sermons and his friends and pupils, to Ficino himself, to Savonarola.

quotes.text: it is no accident that Ficino was, at the start of Savonarola’s reforms, one of his supporters. Thus I see a sense of crisis developing slowly but surely from Caroli, through early sermons of Ficino and some of his friends and pupils, to Ficino himself, to Savonarola.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 29' at l. 1646 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino counted among Savonarola's early supporters, per Edelheit
Ficino's stance toward Savonarola

text: Edelheit says Pico does not stress the feeling of crisis in so many words, but that his demand to treat all theological opinions later than Scripture and the early councils as mere opinion, to be re-examined for probabilitas, is a humanist answer to a crisis of authority in theology, and its essence differs from Ficino's solution.

quotes.text: Pico, on the other hand, does not emphasize, in so many words, the feeling of crisis; but his demand to consider all theological opinions later than Scripture and the early Ecumenical Councils as equally a matter of mere opinion, to be reexamined as to their probabilitas (a term taken from the skeptical Academy), and sometimes reassessed against their historical background, is no less of a humanist solution to what is clearly a crisis of authority in theology. His solution is different in its essence from that of Ficino
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 29' at l. 1646 opens this page

bears_on.note: Differing solutions to a shared crisis

judged.justification: Locates the Pico-Ficino difference in the kind of solution to a crisis of authority.

text: Edelheit says Ficino's arguments in his account of religion are metaphysical and mostly taken from Neoplatonism, in whose translation and dissemination Ficino played a key role, and that his concept of the history of religion is richer and more consistent than the mere use of historical examples in sermons.

quotes.text: Ficino’s concept of history, and especially of the history of religion, is richer and much more consistent than the mere use of historical examples in a sermon, and the metaphysical arguments he employs are more consistent, and new. They are mostly taken from Neoplatonism, in the translation and dissemination of which he played a key role.
quotes.page_basis: running head '30 introduction' at l. 1692 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's Neoplatonic metaphysics as the framework of his theology

text: Edelheit says the Platonic and Neoplatonic writings supplied Ficino with his framework for the history of religion, while for Pico the instrument for a first, philosophical re-examination of religious opinions is the concepts of probabile and verisimile, which he learned by his own admission from the skeptical Academy's writings in Latin.

quotes.text: The Platonic and Neoplatonic writings, recently brought to the West in the fifteenth century, supply Ficino with his framework for the history of religion. For Pico, the basic instrument for a first, philosophical, re-examination of religious opinions are the concepts of probabile and verisimile, which he learnt (on his own admission) from the writings of the skeptical Academy surviving in Latin.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 33' at l. 1832 opens this page

bears_on.note: Different philosophical instruments: Neoplatonism for Ficino, Academic probability for Pico

judged.justification: Distinguishes the philosophical basis of the two projects.

text: Edelheit says that in the Apologia Pico uses two styles: scholastic Latin and argument when refuting the papal commission's scholastic points, and humanist Latin and historically contextual arguments when presenting his own approach to religion.

quotes.text: While refuting some of the scholastic points raised by members of the papal commission, he employs the Latin scholastic style, uses scholastic types of arguments, and refers extensively to scholastic literature. But when he presents his own approach to religion and his own suggestions as to how religious opinions should be re-examined, his Latin becomes humanist Latin
quotes.page_basis: running head '30 introduction' at l. 1692 opens this page

bears_on.note: Pico's scholastic register is the register of his answer to the commission

text: Edelheit says Ficino, and some other humanists, borrowed the concept of ancient theology, prisca theologia, from the Neoplatonic tradition to designate pre-Christian pagan theology culminating in Plato.

quotes.text: ‘Ancient theology’, prisca theologia, was a concept which Ficino, and some other humanists, borrowed from the Neoplatonic tradition to designate pre-Christian, pagan theology, culminating in Plato.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 33' at l. 1832 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's ancient theology comes from the Neoplatonic tradition, per Edelheit

text: Edelheit says that through the influence of Gemistos Plethon Pico planned a work interpreting ancient poetry on a Neoplatonic allegorical basis but did not live to write it.

quotes.text: Through the influence of Gemistos Plethon, Pico also planned a work interpreting ancient poetry on a Neoplatonic allegorical basis—but he did not live to write it.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 33' at l. 1832 opens this page

text: Edelheit says that although Plotinus and Proclus figure largely in Pico's 900 theses, Pico is in no way a Platonist like Ficino, and appears to offer their opinions as further opinions to be examined.

quotes.text: Although Plotinus and Proclus figure largely in the theses, Pico is in no way a Platonist like Ficino, and it seems that he offers their opinions as yet more opinions to be examined.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 47' at l. 2501 opens this page

bears_on.note: Edelheit denies that Pico is a Platonist in Ficino's sense

judged.justification: Reads the Neoplatonic theses as opinions under examination, not as Pico's own Platonism, which reframes the dispute with Ficino as one between a Platonist and a non-Platonist examiner.

text: Edelheit says the Apologia is Pico's theoretical exposition of the reason for publishing the 900 theses without comment, and suggests it was his contribution to the public debate the theses invited, which never took place.

quotes.text: an analysis of Pico’s Apologia as a work of theology is required, since I regard it as Pico’s theoretical exposition of the rationale behind publishing, with no comments, his 900 theses. I also suggest that Pico published his Apologia as his contribution to the public debate suggested by his theses, which never took place.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 47' at l. 2501 opens this page

bears_on.note: The Apologia read as Pico's substitute for the debate that never took place

text: Edelheit says Pico uses the Academy's procedures only at the lower, philosophical level of judging opinions by probability, and remains a Christian who accepts Scripture, the Creed and the first councils as binding and of divine origin.

quotes.text: But Pico is not ‘just’ a skeptical academic. As my analysis shows, he uses the procedures of the Academics only at the lower, philosophical level of examining opinions as to their greater or lesser probability. Pico is a Christian, and he accepts Scripture, the Creed and the dogmatic decisions of the first Ecumenical Councils as binding and of divine origin.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'introduction 47' at l. 2501 opens this page

warrants.text: Rests on Edelheit's own analysis of the Apologia

text: Edelheit says both Ficino and Pico use new and different philosophical approaches to reconstitute Christian theology, and that the new theology each produces is still clearly Christian and Catholic.

quotes.text: Thus, both Ficino and Pico make use of new—and different—philosophical approaches in order to reconstitute Christian theological thought. But the new theology they produce is still clearly Christian and Catholic.
quotes.page_basis: running head '48 introduction' at l. 2552 opens this page

bears_on.note: Different philosophical routes to a Catholic theology

text: Edelheit's footnote reports Garin's remark that Caroli, though he admired Giovanni Pico's very elegant style, did not accept Pico's conclusions and discussed them with his friend Pietro Negro, and notes that Giovanni di Napoli discussed Caroli's critique of Pico's Theses.

quotes.text: e se ammirava lo stile elegantissimo di Giovanni Pico, non ne accettava le conclusioni, e ne discuteva con l’amico Pietro Negro, dolendosi con lui dei tempi moderni, così travagliati.
quotes.page_basis: running head '50 chapter one' at l. 2608 opens this page

quotes.text: Giovanni di Napoli in his Giovanni Pico della Mirandola… p. 144, mentioned and discussed Caroli’s critique of Pico’s Theses.
quotes.page_basis: running head '50 chapter one' at l. 2608 opens this page

text: Edelheit suggests that a passage in Ficino's early sermons on the distinction between animal instinct and human self-directed action may be an important source for the famous words at the beginning of Pico's oration, composed a few years later.

quotes.text: Ficino’s source may be mediaeval, but the distinction between instinct in animals and active reasoning in man is well attested in Stoic sources. This passage might be an important source for Pico’s famous words at the beginning of his oration, which was composed a few years later.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'humanist theology in practice 157' at l. 8140 opens this page

warrants.text: Compares the sermon's account of man choosing his own course with Pico's Adam passage, which Edelheit quotes in a note

open_questions.text: Whether Ficino's sermon passage lies behind the Oration's opening is offered only as a possibility

basis_quote.text: This passage might be an important source

bears_on.note: Ficino's sermon as a possible source for the Oration's account of man

judged.justification: Proposes a textual link from Ficino's sermon to the Oration.

text: Edelheit says that in Ficino's sermon on Christ's temptation the three hierarchies of angels are equated to the three levels of evangelical truth, a use of angelic orders as an exegetical scheme.

quotes.text: The three hierarchies of angels which are equated to the three levels of evangelical truth have an important role to play:
quotes.page_basis: running head '152 chapter two' at l. 7878 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's use of the angelic hierarchies as a scheme of the Gospel's levels of meaning

text: Edelheit says Ficino's sermon on Paul's rapture draws on Hebrew philosophers, Dionysius the Areopagite and Thomas Aquinas, and that Thomas and Augustine are the only late Christian sources Ficino employs in the sermons, probably because of their unique status.

quotes.text: The rest of this sermon is devoted to this explanation and contains references to Hebrew philosophers, Dionysius the Areopagite and Thomas Aquinas.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'humanist theology in practice 165' at l. 8549 opens this page

quotes.text: Thomas and Augustine are the only late Christian sources employed by Ficino, probably because of their unique status.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'humanist theology in practice 165' at l. 8549 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino cites Dionysius and Aquinas on angels in a sermon

text: Edelheit says that Ficino's sermon on Paul's suffering attributes incredulity to demons rather than to the humours and says angels strengthen faith, and that Ficino's theology cannot be separated from his philosophy, cosmology and medicine.

quotes.text: Ficino claims that although many sins are caused by the humours, incredulitas is not one of them, since it is caused instead by demons. Angels, on the other hand, strengthen our faith. It is not possible to separate Ficino’s theology from his philosophy, cosmology, and medicine.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'humanist theology in practice 163' at l. 8449 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's demonology and angelology within a Neoplatonic cosmology

text: Edelheit observes that in Ficino's sermons the human soul is a third nature inclined both up and down, temporal through the senses and eternal through the intellect, set between the mortal nature of animals and the eternal nature of angels, and calls this a Neoplatonic framework with Christian influences rather than Aristotelian physics.

quotes.text: In the first part of the first sermon, Ficino distinguishes between two different natures: temporal, heavy, corporeal, and mortal in animals; light and eternal in angels.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'humanist theology in practice 149' at l. 7723 opens this page

quotes.text: This is our human soul, which through its senses is temporal, and through its intellect is eternal. Here we are no longer in the ... realm of Aristotelian physics but rather in a Neoplatonic framework with Christian influences.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'humanist theology in practice 149' at l. 7723 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's placing of the soul between the animal and angelic natures

text: Edelheit says Ficino's prisca theologia was intended to replace the Aristotelian metaphysics that had played a dominant role in scholastic theology.

quotes.text: This interest was expressed in terms of a prisca theologia, which was intended to replace the Aristotelian metaphysics that had played a dominant role in scholastic theology.
quotes.page_basis: running head '206 chapter three' at l. 10593 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's programme sets Platonic ancient theology against Aristotelian scholastic metaphysics

judged.justification: Places Ficino's Platonism as a programmatic alternative to scholastic Aristotelianism, the ground on which Pico later contends.

text: Edelheit says Ficino calls for replacing the Aristotelian foundation of scholastic theology with an ancient Neoplatonic theology serving as a preamble of faith, on the model of Augustine, and regards this as what Ficino means by legitimate wisdom.

quotes.text: On the one hand, he is calling for the replacement of the Aristotelian foundation of scholastic theology by an ancient Neoplatonic theology, which should serve as praeambula fidei, similar to Augustine’s model; this is what he regards as the “legitimate wisdom”.
quotes.page_basis: running head '256 chapter three' at l. 13161 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's Platonic replacement of scholastic Aristotelianism

text: Edelheit suspects that Ficino's discussions of prisca theologia may be aimed at professional theologians such as Caroli, indicating to them that Platonism is more relevant to understanding Christianity than the traditional Aristotelianism of the scholastics.

quotes.text: I suspect that the discussions of prisca theologia, beside being part of Ficino’s own conception of the continuity and break in the history of religion, may also be directed at professional theologians such as Caroli. The connection which Ficino establishes between prisca theologia and early Platonism, and between early Christianity and late Platonism, may serve as an indication to them that Platonism is more relevant to the understanding of Christianity and of religion in general than the traditional Aristotelianism of the scholastics.
quotes.page_basis: running head '258 chapter three' at l. 13262 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's Platonism offered to scholastic theologians as an alternative to Aristotle

text: Edelheit says the ancient theologians are in harmony with one another for Ficino and are all represented in Plato, who is interpreted by Neoplatonists who adopted the mysteries of Christianity, so that Christianity is the climax of the histories of both religion and philosophy.

quotes.text: the ancient theologians are in harmony with one another, and they all are represented in Plato; Plato is interpreted by those Neoplatonic philosophers who used and adopted the mysterious truths of Christianity. Since the praecipua mysteria of the late Platonists are based on John, Paul, Hierotheus, and Dionysius the Areopagite, Christianity is the climax of both the history of religion and the history of philosophy.
quotes.page_basis: running head '234 chapter three' at l. 12041 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's account of how the late Platonists depend on Dionysius and Hierotheus

judged.justification: Explains Ficino's Neoplatonism as historically dependent on Christian sources, including Dionysius.

text: Edelheit says Ficino claims to have found that the chief mysteries of Numenius, Philo, Plotinus, Iamblichus and Proclus were taken from John, Paul, Hierotheus and Dionysius the Areopagite, and that whatever they said about the divine mind and the angels was taken from those figures.

quotes.text: Ego certe reperi praecipua Numenii, Philonis, Plotini, Iamblici, Proculi mysteria, ab Ioanne, Paulo, Yerotheo, Dionysio Areopagita accepta fuisse. Quicquid enim de mente divina angelisque, et caeteris ad Theologiam spectantibus magniﬁcum dixere, manifeste ab illis usurpaverunt.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'marsilio ficino and the conditioreligionis 233' at l. 11991 opens this page

quotes.text: Ficino admits that he is developing the arguments or cultural programme of Basil and Augustine regarding the usurpatio and acceptio of the ideas of John, Paul, Hierotheus, and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in the philosophical writings of Numenius, Philo, Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus.
quotes.page_basis: running head 'marsilio ficino and the conditioreligionis 233' at l. 11991 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino's own account of the Christian origin of late Platonic teaching on mind and angels

judged.justification: Shows Ficino claiming the Platonists' doctrine of mind and angels as borrowed from Dionysius, a datum for any comparison with Pico's use of Dionysius.

text: Edelheit says Basil and Augustine confirm only that the Platonists used the mysteries of John the Evangelist, so that Ficino, who names Basil and Augustine, is placing this idea in his own cultural programme after centuries in which the Greek Neoplatonists had hardly been known in the Latin West.

quotes.text: But Basil and Augustine confirm only that the Platonists—a very general and vague name—used the mysteries of John the Evangelist. Ficino places this idea in his own cultural programme, and he is doing so after hundreds of years in which these Greek authors and this philosophical tradition had hardly been known in the Latin West
quotes.page_basis: running head 'marsilio ficino and the conditioreligionis 233' at l. 11991 opens this page

bears_on.note: Ficino extends a patristic claim beyond what Basil and Augustine said

judged.justification: Marks the step from the Fathers' modest claim to Ficino's own historical thesis.

text: Edelheit reports Allen's view that Ficino's programme differed from Augustine's and was more radical: to champion Platonism not as a stepping stone but as an integral, complementary theology given to the gentiles like a gentile Old Testament, with Plotinus, the arch interpreter, taking centre stage or sharing it with Plato.

quotes.text: … Ficino’s programme emerged as something different from Augustine’s and in intention certainly as much more radical. His aim was to champion Platonism, not merely as stepping stone to conversion, a propaedeutic to be cast aside eventually in the rapture of belief, but as an alternative, integral, and complementary theology, a theology granted by God to the gentiles and constituting a gentile Old Testament that contained, like its Hebraic counterpart, intimations or adumbrations of the mysteries of the New. In this scenario, interestingly, it is the arch interpreter, Plotinus, who takes centre stage or at least shares it with Plato, the authority to be interpreted.
quotes.page_basis: running head '234 chapter three' at l. 12041 opens this page

quotes.text: Pico does not offer in his Apologia a completely new system of religion and theology. This is also out of character for Pico. He is not mainly a man who wishes to introduce a new way of thinking to his generation. He would rather deal with individual issues as they come. Nine hundred theses, or even a discussion of one central philosophical problem as we have it in De ente et uno, are a far cry from De Christiana religione, Theologia platonica, and the gigantic project of translation and interpretation of the whole corpus of Plato and Plotinus, and some works of later Platonists.

text: Edelheit summarises the sequence: in 1486 Pico planned a council in Rome to dispute nine hundred theses, including Neoplatonic and Kabbalistic material; some theologians had him suspected of heresy; a papal commission found thirteen theses heretical or of dubious orthodoxy; and the Apologia of 1487 answered the condemnation of those thirteen.

quotes.text: In 1486 Pico returned to Florence from his theological studies in Paris. Here he had a new and original plan: to organize an international council in Rome and to invite to it the best philosophers and theologians, to discuss and dispute nine hundred theological and philosophical theses which he collected from many sources. These theses included much material which was new to Western Europe, taken from Neoplatonic sources such as Plotinus and Proclus, and from the Jewish Kabbalah.
the commission found thirteen heretical or of dubious orthodoxy. Pico’s Apologia, which he published in 1487 was his answer to the condemnation of these thirteen theses.

bears_on.note: Edelheit's summary of the commission's finding of thirteen theses

text: Edelheit says that on the issue of authority in philosophy and theology the positions of Ficino and Pico are not all that different: what Ficino does by selecting and omitting sources, Pico does explicitly by critical discussion of Doctors and Fathers and by rejecting the authoritative status of their opinions.

quotes.text: I shall only emphasize again that on the issue of authority in matters of philosophy and theology their positions are not all that different. What Ficino does by the selection of the sources he quotes and mentions and the omission of references to scholastic and to most patristic sources, Pico does explicitly by his critical discussions of the opinions of various Doctors and Fathers and by his general rejection of the authoritative status of such opinions.

quotes.text: Both Ficino and Pico represent the evolution of a new humanist theology, which rejects most of the mediaeval tradition, returns to Scripture and early Christianity, and introduces materials from newly discovered texts, especially of Plato and the Neoplatonists. This introduction of materials which were new to the Latin West, including even Hebrew and Arabic sources, into Christian theology is done by Pico in his nine hundred theses.

text: Edelheit gives the chronology of the affair: the commission's denunciation of thirteen theses on March 13, 1487, three of them heretical; publication of the Apologia on May 31, 1487; Pico's oath on July 31, 1487 to accept the pope's future decision; and the pope's denunciation of the theses on August 4, 1487.

quotes.text: On March 13, 1487, the papal commission denounced, without a full agreement between its members, thirteen theses. This denunciation was on different levels of gravity but three of them were considered heretical. On May 31, 1487, Pico published his Apologia.

On July 31, 1487, Pico swore to accept the future decision of the pope regarding his theses. On August 4, 1487, the pope denounced the theses and prohibited to publish, to read, to hear, and to destribute them, punishable by excommunication.

text: Edelheit says the theologians of the commission mostly did not read Greek, and that the twenty-four-year-old Pico, though not a professional theologian, showed familiarity with the Latin and Greek Church Fathers, scholastic theology and Greek philosophy from Plato and Aristotle to the Neoplatonists including Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus and Dionysius the Areopagite.

quotes.text: Most of them did not read Greek and could not follow the arguments and ideas in a book whose author—despite his young age (24) and although he was not a professional theologian—showed exceptional familiarity not only with the Latin Church Fathers and scholastic theology, but also with the Greek Church Fathers and with Greek philosophy from Plato and Aristotle up to the Neoplatonist tradition (e.g. Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, Dionysius the Areopagite).

text: Edelheit's view of the purpose of the nine hundred theses is that Pico was putting forward a deliberate critique of scholastic theology, confronting the Church and demanding a decision on a vast range of opinions in order to produce a historical-critical perspective.

quotes.text: In my view, he was putting forward a deliberate critique of scholastic theology. This critique was aimed at confronting the Church and demanding a decision on a vast range of opinions, in order to produce a historical-critical perspective, which emphasized that these opinions had arisen in different cultural contexts, rather than deriving directly from faith.

judged.justification: Reads the 900 theses as a strategic critique of scholastic theology rather than a syncretic system.

text: Edelheit says Pico offered concordia as the criterion for judging opinions, reached by systematic critical analysis of all human knowledge with reason, experience, authority of authors, and historical and philological analysis, and then a higher concordia between the tested opinions and scriptural faith.

quotes.text: Pico offered the concept of concordia as the criterion for judging opinions in this examination. We reach this concordia, which constitutes a new relationship between opinio and fides, by means of a systematic discussion and critical analysis of all human knowledge using the best human instruments: reason, experience, and the authority of other authors, historical and philological analysis of the different sources and contexts.
At the final stage, this should be a concordia between opiniones which have stood the philosophical test, on the one hand, and scriptural fides, on the other.

warrants.text: Edelheit's own analysis of the Apologia

judged.justification: Recasts Pico's concordia as an epistemic criterion for sorting opinions, not a doctrine of the agreement of Plato and Aristotle.

quotes.text: The principle of concordia, achieved in two stages of the examination of theological and philosophical opinions—this was Pico’s original contribution to the theological crisis of his age: the crisis of ultimate authority in matters of faith.

judged.justification: Presents concordia as Pico's distinctive contribution.
